name: Cold compress for red eyes

lead: Holding something cold against the eyelids is a common quick fix for puffy or red-looking eyes. People use it before going out for a fresher look that lasts a while.

Cold on the face causes vasoconstriction in physiology tests, which is the usual reasoning given for reduced redness and swelling. One small trial examined cold compresses for induced allergic eye symptoms; none have measured cosmetic whiteness.

paras: Users rest a chilled cloth, gel pack or cold spoons on closed lids for a few minutes, often in the morning or just before an event. The effect is described as temporary.

Clinical references list many causes of red eye, some urgent such as angle-closure glaucoma, so persistent or painful redness is a medical matter. Ice should not be pressed directly on the skin for long.

angle.text: A chilled cloth on the closed lids narrows blood vessels and cuts puffiness and redness within minutes, so the eyes look fresher for a while. A small trial has tested it for allergic eye itch.

lead: A cold compress for red eyes is a chilled cloth, gel mask, spoon or pack held against closed eyelids to make eyes look less puffy and less irritated for a short time. People use it before photos, events or work as a quick way to look more rested, and some use it after crying, late nights or allergy flare-ups.[1]

The usual reasoning is that cold narrows blood vessels and limits fluid in the tissue, which reduces visible puffiness and flushing. Wikipedia's article on periorbital puffiness presents cold compresses as a short-term fix, attributing the explanation to a beauty-advice book.[2] Physiology research shows that cold applied to the face produces bradycardia and peripheral vasoconstriction, known as the diving reflex.[3]

Clinical references list many causes of red eye, from allergic and viral conjunctivitis to dry eye and blepharitis. A small randomised trial tested cold compresses, alone and with artificial tears, in induced allergic conjunctivitis.[1]
infobox: Chilled cloth, gel mask, cold spoons, ice pack

paras: The approach uses a chilled object held against closed eyelids or the skin around the eyes. Proponents describe it as a way to narrow blood vessels and reduce swelling quickly, and it appears in everyday beauty routines for morning puffiness.[2] Wikipedia's article on periorbital puffiness lists elevating the head during sleep and diet changes as other approaches and lists allergies, sleep loss, crying, sodium intake and age as common contributors to puffiness.[2]

Cold therapy more broadly is described as lowering tissue temperature, triggering cycles of vessel narrowing and widening, and reducing swelling; it is widely used after injuries and surgery.[4] Sources on cold therapy also note that ice applied directly to skin can cause burns, which is why wrapped or gel packs with time limits are recommended.[4]

Wikipedia's article on conjunctivitis lists causes of red eye including viral, bacterial, allergic and chemical conjunctivitis, as well as corneal abrasion, dry eye, blepharitis, keratitis, uveitis and acute angle-closure glaucoma, the last being urgent. It describes allergic cases as sometimes eased by artificial tears or antihistamines. A systematic review of guidelines for conjunctivitis covers recommended management across infectious and non-infectious forms.[5]

Cold compresses appear in forum posts mainly as part of recovery routines. One T Nation member described assembling a small kit that included cold compresses for the eyes, mint tea and electrolyte packets for the aftermath of a night out.[6] This is a mention in passing rather than a protocol.

A randomised, masked trial of 18 grass-pollen-allergic adults tested artificial tears and a cold compress, alone or in combination, after exposure in an environmental chamber, comparing them with topical antiallergic medication.[1] Studies of the cold face test describe the cardiovascular responses to facial cold exposure.[3] No studies found testing cold compresses for cosmetic eye whiteness or under-eye puffiness in healthy people.

lore.intro: Cold compresses are mentioned in passing in recovery routines; community material specific to red eyes is limited.[6]
